approachQuestion.prompt:
Watchtower Layouts

Place n towers on an n by n board, exactly one per row. Towers cannot share a column or either diagonal. Some squares are blocked. Return every layout as a length-n vector of column indices, once, in any order. Towers have no individual identities.

Examples:
n=4, blocked=[] -> [[1,3,0,2],[2,0,3,1]].
n=1, blocked=[(0,0)] -> [].

Constraints: 1 <= n <= 11. A supplied n by n boolean blocked matrix supports direct lookup; the examples name its true cells. Diagonal means equal row-column or equal row+column.

options.text: Build one row at a time, testing a column flag and two indexed diagonal flags before placing each tower. Undo exactly those flags on return and emit only complete vectors.
options.feedback: Rows are distinct by construction. The three flags represent precisely the remaining conflicts, so every valid vector is reachable without rescanning placed towers.

options.text: Track only used columns because each row is already unique.
options.feedback: For n=2 with no blocked cells this accepts [0,1], whose towers share the main diagonal.

options.text: Once a diagonal is marked, keep it marked even after removing the tower that introduced it.
options.feedback: On an empty n=4 board, early failed prefixes would permanently block diagonals needed by the two valid solutions.

options.text: Use the same row search but test every new square against all previously placed towers by scanning their coordinates.
options.feedback: This is correct, but indexed diagonal and column flags remove repeated scans of the prefix.

feedback.reason: Rows are distinct by construction. The three flags represent precisely the remaining conflicts, so every valid vector is reachable without rescanning placed towers.
details: Allocate column and two diagonal occupancy arrays. Process rows in order; scan all columns and choose any unblocked square with all three occupancy flags clear. Set flags, recurse, and clear them on return. Copy the column vector after n rows.

One tower per processed row leaves only column and two diagonal conflicts to track. Set all three flags before descent and clear them afterward. Equal row count alone does not prove diagonal compatibility.

“Build one row at a time, testing a column flag and two indexed diagonal flags before placing each tower. Undo exactly those flags on return and emit only complete vectors.”: Rows are distinct by construction. The three flags represent precisely the remaining conflicts, so every valid vector is reachable without rescanning placed towers.
“Track only used columns because each row is already unique.”: For n=2 with no blocked cells this accepts [0,1], whose towers share the main diagonal.

“Once a diagonal is marked, keep it marked even after removing the tower that introduced it.”: On an empty n=4 board, early failed prefixes would permanently block diagonals needed by the two valid solutions.

“Use the same row search but test every new square against all previously placed towers by scanning their coordinates.”: This is correct, but indexed diagonal and column flags remove repeated scans of the prefix.

complexityQuestion.prompt: Analyze `acm-b18-13-search` only. Let I be the number of nonterminal calls, and R the number of column indices copied into returned layouts. Each nonterminal call scans all n columns, using constant-time input/flag checks. Initialize linear-length flag arrays. Terminal calls copy n entries. Choose the tightest stated time and auxiliary-space pair. Count recursion and mutable working state; exclude supplied input and returned output storage, but include copying work in time. Primitive integer/index operations and preallocated-array updates cost constant time; dynamic appends are amortized constant time. No hashing is used unless explicitly stated.

options.text: O(n + n·I + R) time, O(n) auxiliary space
O(n + I + R) time, O(n) auxiliary space
O(n + n·I + R) time, O(n²) auxiliary space
O(n² + R) time, O(n) auxiliary space

feedback.reason: Each nonterminal state checks n columns; complete layouts add output-copy work.
details: Initialization costs n. Every nonterminal call performs exactly n candidate checks; terminal copying costs R and absorbs terminal overhead.
Column and diagonal arrays have linear length, as do the working vector and depth-n stack. The blocked matrix is input.

Let I be the number of nonterminal calls, and R the number of column indices copied into returned layouts. Each nonterminal call scans all n columns, using constant-time input/flag checks. Initialize linear-length flag arrays. Terminal calls copy n entries.
“O(n + I + R) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: This omits n column checks per nonterminal call.
“O(n + n·I + R) time, O(n²) auxiliary space”: Only flag arrays are allocated; the blocked matrix is supplied input.
“O(n² + R) time, O(n) auxiliary space”: The recursive search can visit many row prefixes, not only n rows once.
